source_text: Ut autem ad istam commemorationem humanae miseriae et divinae gratiae veniret Apostolus supra dixerat: Video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meae, et captivantem me in lege peccati [n155] ; post haec verba exclamavit: Quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius? Gratia Dei per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum [n156] . Constat quidem praemissis illis quae posuisti, subdidisse Apostolum: Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius? Gratia Dei per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Sed non quaerimus impraesentiarum, utrum hoc Apostolus dixerit; verum qua fide, quo sensu, qua ratione dixerit quaerimus. Ille enim in membris legem per flagitiorum usum sanctis consiliis inter principia tamen emendationis rebellem, consuetudinem malam vocabat, quae ab eruditis etiam saeculi dici solet secunda natura. Ante pauca enim eos, ad quos loquitur, cum exprobratione conveniens dixerat: Humanum est quod dico, propter infirmitatem carnis vestrae; sicut enim exhibuistis membra vestra servire immunditiae et iniquitati ad iniquitatem; ita nunc exhibete membra vestra servire iustitiae in sanctificationem [n157] . Utque ostenderet quia carnem, non hoc corpus quod causas in seminibus habet, sed vitia abusive vocaret; post duo capita fortasse subiungit: Cum essemus in carne, passiones peccatorum quae per legem ostenduntur, operabantur in membris nostris, ut fructificarent morti [n158] . Sic dixit: Cum essemus in carne, quasi eo tempore cum disputaret, in carne non esset; sed qui Scripturas novit, genus hoc elocutionis agnoscit. Et ideo, ubi verborum communitas ingerit quaestionem, adhibeatur regula rationis, ad cuius aequalitatem, quae putabantur deflexisse, tendantur. Ceterum Faustus, Manichaeorum episcopus, praeceptor tuus, hoc vel maxime Apostoli testimonio contra nos nititur, dicens ab eo nihil aliud his sermonibus, legis videlicet quae repugnans consilio in membris habitet, quam naturam malam significatam fuisse. Unde nihil minus a te fieri debuit, quam hic locus sic intellegi, quomodo ab illis exponitur, ne, cum per easdem lineas, quas Faustus torsit, ingrederis, non disputasse, sed praeterita reddidisse videaris.
pass_a_gloss: But that the Apostle might come to that recalling of human misery and of divine grace he had said above: I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind, and capturing me in the law of sin; after these words he exclaimed: Who will free me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. It stands indeed that to those premises which you placed, the Apostle subjected: Wretched I a human, who will free me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. But we do not ask at present whether the Apostle said this; but with what faith, with what sense, with what reason he said it we ask. For he was calling a law in the members, rebellious to holy counsels through the use of shameful deeds at least in the beginnings of amendment, a bad custom, which even by the learned of the age is accustomed to be called a second nature. For a few things before, convening those to whom he speaks with reproach, he had said: It is human what I say, on account of the infirmity of your flesh; for as you exhibited your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity; so now exhibit your members to serve justice unto sanctification. And that he might show that he was calling flesh, not this body which has causes in seeds, but vices abusively; after perhaps two heads he joins: When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which are shown through the law were working in our members, that they might bear fruit to death. Thus he said: When we were in the flesh, as if at that time when he was disputing he were not in the flesh; but he who has known the Scriptures recognizes this kind of expression. And therefore, where a community of words brings in a question, let the rule of reason be applied, to whose evenness those things which were thought to have bent may be stretched. For the rest Faustus, bishop of the Manichaeans, your teacher, leans especially by this testimony of the Apostle against us, saying that by him nothing other by these speeches, namely of a law which dwelling in the members fights the counsel, was signified than an evil nature. Whence nothing less ought to have been done by you, than that this place be so understood, in the way it is expounded by them, lest, when you enter through the same lines which Faustus twisted, you seem not to have disputed, but to have given back things past.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: “To arrive at this mention of human misery and divine grace, the apostle had said earlier: ‘I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin’ (Romans 7:23). After these words he exclaimed: ‘Who will rescue me from the body of this death? God's grace through Jesus Christ our Lord’” (Romans 7:24–25). It is indeed established that after the preceding words you quoted, the apostle added: “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from the body of this death? God's grace through Jesus Christ our Lord.” But at present we are not asking whether the apostle said this. We are asking with what belief, meaning, and reasoning he said it. By the law in his members he meant an evil habit that, through the practice of shameful deeds, rebels against holy intentions, at least in the beginning of amendment. Even learned people of this world commonly call habit a second nature.

A little earlier, addressing his readers reproachfully, he had said: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and lawlessness leading to lawlessness, so now present your members to serve righteousness leading to sanctification” (Romans 6:19). To show that by “flesh” he figuratively meant vices, not this body whose causes lie in seed, he adds perhaps two passages later: “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which are disclosed through the Law worked in our members to bear fruit for death” (Romans 7:5). He said, “When we were in the flesh”, as though he were not in the flesh at the time he was speaking. But whoever knows Scripture recognizes this manner of expression. Where a shared use of words creates a difficulty, therefore, apply the rule of reason, and let what seemed bent be straightened against its level.

Faustus, bishop of the Manichaeans and your teacher, relies especially on this testimony of the apostle against us. He says that by these words about a law dwelling in the members and resisting the mind's purpose, the apostle meant nothing other than an evil nature. Nothing, therefore, was less appropriate for you than to understand this passage as they explain it. Otherwise, as you follow the same twisted lines Faustus drew, you seem not to have argued a case but to have recited old lessons.
